title: Music that moves
hookLine: music can stop a person in the middle of a day: listen to one piece all the way through

lines: A SONG IN THE CEREAL AISLE.
ONE PIECE, ALL THE WAY THROUGH.
cards: A song comes on in a grocery store, and for no reason anyone else can see, someone in the cereal aisle has to stop and hold the shelf. It's a song from a wedding, or a funeral, or a car ride years ago.

Three notes in, and they're somewhere else. Music turns up in temples and churches and gurdwaras, at weddings and wakes, on kitchen radios and in headphones on the night bus. And yet it's often just background.
Today, music in the foreground: one piece, all the way through.

teach.b: First, a harp in a troubled room. In the First Book of Samuel, King Saul is tormented by what the text calls an evil spirit. His servants send for a young shepherd who can play the harp.
His name is David. When the trouble came on Saul, the text says, David played, and Saul was refreshed and was well, and the evil spirit left him. The story doesn't explain how.
It just says the music helped. Second, a reed that cries. The Masnavi, the long poem of the Persian mystic Rumi, opens with a reed flute.

teach.h: RUMI'S REED: A SONG OF LONGING.
teach.b: The reed was cut from its reed bed, the poem says, and that's why its song sounds like longing: it's crying to go home.
Some readers have heard the reed as the human soul, separated from its source, and every song as a kind of homesickness. Third, everything that breathes.
In the King James Bible, the Book of Psalms ends with a psalm full of music: trumpet, harp, timbrel, strings, organs, loud cymbals.

teach.h: PSALM 150: EVERY THING THAT HATH BREATH.
teach.b: Then the last verse: "Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD." Breath itself, turned into song. Fourth, why the whole piece.
A clip gives you the mood.

teach.h: THE WHOLE PIECE IS A JOURNEY.
teach.b: The whole piece gives you the journey: where it starts, where it wanders, how it comes home.

teach.h: LET EVERY THING THAT HATH BREATH.
teach.b: Listening to the end, without skipping, is a small act of trust. You let someone else's sound carry you, and see where you land.

how: Music is part of worship and devotion on several paths, from psalms and hymns to Sufi poetry and kirtan; some people make a practice of listening to one piece of music fully, without doing anything else.

o: Rumi's long poem, which opens with a crying reed flute
the reed flute that Sufi musicians play in worship
a Persian word for the longing to go home

games.q: you're Saul's servant. the king is tormented and nothing helps. what do you send for?
o: a young man who can play the harp.
a scholar to argue with the king.
games.why: they send for David and his harp, and the text says Saul was refreshed when he played.

practice: Choose one piece of music, a hymn, a chant, a song from your childhood, something with no words at all, then put it on and do nothing else.
Follow one thread, a voice, a drum, a single instrument, and if you like, let it play past the bell to its last note. If you pray, music can be part of that; if you don't, simply let it carry you.

wordCard.voice: Masnavi. Rumi's long poem that opens with a reed flute longing for home, alongside a harp for a troubled king and a psalm of breath. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the music. Three notes can carry a person a long way. One thousand forty-one days now.
